scenes.title: Cold open
narration: The Clappers of Khandara
This is Dasakathia. Traditional (Living).

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Dasakathia is believed to have originated in Khandara village, located in the Ganjam district of Odisha.
It historically served as a primary form of entertainment in Odia culture, where travelling performers would move from village to village.
The performers traditionally view themselves as 'Dasa' or devotees of Lord Shiva.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Originally a religious performance dedicated to Lord Shiva, it now encompasses a wide range of subjects including mythology, romance, and social satire.
It is used for entertainment and, increasingly, for public service announcements by the government to reach rural populations.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The performance is a duo act involving a lead (Gayaka) and a follower (Palia).

While specific step-by-step choreography is not detailed in the sources, it is classified as a performing art and dance where the artists use wooden instruments—the Ramtali and Dasakathi—to create a rhythmic accompaniment to their movements and singing.
The performers engage in a call-and-response format that involves physical gestures and rhythmic coordination.
Watch for Kathia playing.

Formation: Two performers (Gayaka and Palia) standing in close proximity, usually on a stage or public square.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The music is based on traditional Odissi music.
Two specific wooden percussion instruments are used: the Ramtali, held by the Gayaka, and the Dasakathi, held by the Palia.
Listen for the Ramtali, Dasakathi (wooden clappers).

A sharp, rhythmic clicking of wooden instruments provides the pulse for a two-person vocal dialogue. The lead singer provides the melody and narrative, while the second performer provides a rhythmic and vocal echo, creating a layered, percussive folk sound.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Gayakratna Baidyanath Sharma is cited as a notable performer who has contributed to the art form in recent times.
While primarily associated with the Ganjam district, it is performed throughout the state of Odisha as a representative folk art.
Dasakathia is a subclass of Odisha folk dance and Indian folk music, sharing a generic lineage with Odissi music traditions.
